title: The Lesson I Learned From the Extra Oil
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Extra Oil
The Door Did Not Close Because They Were Wicked. It Closed Because They Were Unprepared.
There is a sound I cannot stop hearing whenever I read Jesus' parable of the ten virgins.
It is not the sound of celebration.
It is not the music of the wedding feast.
It is the sound of a closed door.
A door that once stood open.
A door that invited everyone to come.
A door that patiently waited.
A door that eventually shut.
And what makes this story so unsettling is that the people left outside were not strangers to the wedding.
They were expecting it.
They believed it was coming.
They carried lamps.
They looked like everyone else.
Yet five entered and five remained outside.
Not because they hated the bridegroom.
Not because they openly rebelled.
Not because they denied his existence.
They were shut out because they neglected something they thought they could deal with later.
Oil.

Jesus tells the story in Matthew 25:1-13. In the original Greek text, the wise virgins brought extra oil, described as "ἔλαιον" (elaion), olive oil. The foolish carried lamps but no reserve. Everything looked fine while there was still daylight. Everything appeared equal while the bridegroom delayed.
But delays reveal what appearances conceal.
That may be one of the most painful lessons of the Christian life.
Many people look spiritually alive when circumstances are easy.
Many appear strong while the sun is shining.
Many seem devoted when emotions are high.
Many seem prepared when no real testing has arrived.
But delays expose reality.
Waiting exposes reality.
Silence exposes reality.
Suffering exposes reality.
The foolish virgins discovered that borrowed appearances cannot replace personal preparation.
When darkness came, their lamps began to fail.
Suddenly what seemed unimportant became everything.
Suddenly what seemed minor became urgent.
Suddenly what could have been prepared for yesterday became a crisis today.
And I realized something uncomfortable.
Most of us are not afraid of rebellion.
We are afraid of surrender.
We know the obvious sins to avoid.
We know the right words to say.
We know how to attend church.
We know how to post Bible verses.
We know how to look ready.
The danger is that we begin trusting the lamp while neglecting the oil.
The lamp is visible.
The oil is hidden.
The lamp is public.
The oil is private.
The lamp is what people see.
The oil is who you are when nobody is watching.
The oil is the prayer nobody heard.
The repentance nobody applauded.
The obedience nobody celebrated.
The Scripture you read when there was no audience.
The worship offered through tears.
The trust that remained after disappointment.
The faithfulness that survived delay.

Throughout Scripture, oil often symbolizes consecration, God's presence, and spiritual readiness. While Jesus does not explicitly define the oil in this parable, the larger biblical picture consistently points toward a genuine relationship with God rather than external religion.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity has never been about appearing close to Christ.
It has always been about knowing Him.
When the late arrivals finally reached the door, they cried out, "Lord, Lord, open to us."
His response is among the most sobering statements in all Scripture:
"Truly, I say to you, I do not know you." (Matthew 25:12)
The Greek phrase is "οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς" (ouk oida hymas).
Not merely intellectual knowledge.
Relational knowledge.
Intimate recognition.
The issue was not information.
The issue was relationship.
And suddenly the parable becomes deeply personal.
Because there are people who know church but do not know Christ.
People who know theology but do not know Christ.
People who know Christian culture but do not know Christ.
People who can discuss Jesus without ever surrendering to Jesus.
The extra oil was never about earning salvation.
Salvation has always been by grace through faith.
The extra oil reveals whether faith was genuine.
Whether the relationship was real.
Whether preparation was taken seriously.
Whether the heart belonged to the Bridegroom.
That truth becomes even more beautiful when viewed through the lens of the Gospel.
Because every one of us has experienced some form of spiritual scandal.
Maybe not the scandal that made headlines.
But the hidden scandal of pride.
The scandal of lust.
The scandal of bitterness.
The scandal of hypocrisy.
The scandal of selfishness.
The scandal of pretending we are stronger than we really are.
The Hebrew word for sin, "חטא" (chata), literally carries the idea of missing the mark.
And if we are honest, every one of us has missed it.
Every one of us has failed.
Every one of us has run dry.
Every one of us has discovered moments when our lamps flickered.
That is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Jesus did not come looking for perfect people.
He came for broken people.
He came for exhausted people.
He came for sinners.
He came for failures.
He came for people whose stories looked beyond repair.
The cross stands as God's declaration that no scandal is greater than His grace.
At Calvary, Jesus carried our sin.
He absorbed our judgment.
He paid our debt.
Then He rose again, proving that grace has the final word.
This is why our message remains the same:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrote the story of Peter after denial.
He rewrote the story of Paul after persecution.
He rewrote the story of the woman caught in adultery.
He rewrote the story of the thief on the cross.
And He is still rewriting stories today.
Maybe yours.
Maybe the story nobody knows.
Maybe the chapter you are ashamed to discuss.
Maybe the wound you have hidden for years.
Maybe the failure you believe disqualifies you.
Jesus specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
But the parable reminds us that grace is not an excuse for spiritual neglect.
Grace awakens readiness.
Grace produces devotion.
Grace creates watchfulness.
Grace teaches us to treasure the Bridegroom above everything else.
The lesson I learned from the extra oil is simple but unforgettable:
The most important things in your spiritual life are often the things nobody sees.
Not the platform.
Not the applause.
Not the appearance.
But the hidden relationship with Jesus that sustains you when darkness falls.
One day the waiting will end.
One day faith will become sight.
One day the Bridegroom will come.
And on that day, the question will not be how impressive our lamps looked.
The question will be whether we truly knew Him.
If this message stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Sometimes one shared message becomes the moment God uses to change a life forever.
It helps spread biblical truth, Gospel-centered content, discipleship resources, and Christ-exalting messages to more people around the world.
Because one day every earthly light will fade, but those who truly know the Bridegroom will step into a celebration that never ends.
